fields.definition: A curated collection of multisampled piano recordings — typically captured at many pitches and velocity layers, with released and pedal-resonance samples — packaged for playback in a sampler or dedicated virtual instrument.
fields.plain_english: A piano library is a big set of recordings made from a real piano. You load it into music software so your keyboard can sound like that piano.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a musician play a realistic acoustic or electric piano tone from a controller without a physical instrument, by mapping recorded notes across the keyboard. It exists because a single sampled note cannot capture the timbral changes across pitch and dynamics that real pianos produce.
fields.practical_application: A technician loads the library into a sampler, sets the disk-streaming and RAM options for the machine, and adjusts velocity mapping and pedal-resonance settings to fit the mix and CPU budget.
common_mistakes: Assuming one recorded note can be stretched across the whole keyboard without audible artifacts, instead of using many sampled pitches
Loading the full uncompressed library into RAM when disk streaming would use far less memory
Ignoring velocity layers, so soft and loud playing sound identical
scenario_contexts: Producing a pop ballad that needs a convincing acoustic grand piano part
Scoring to picture where a live piano session is not budgeted
Live performance using a MIDI controller and laptop instead of hauling a real piano

fields.definition: A sample loop mode that plays the looped region forward to its end, then backward to its start, alternating direction indefinitely (also called a bidirectional or alternating loop) rather than jumping straight back to the loop start.
fields.plain_english: A ping-pong loop plays a short sound forward, then backward, over and over. It bounces back and forth like a ball, so a held note can keep going smoothly.
fields.purpose_function: It sustains a sampled sound for as long as a key is held while avoiding the click or discontinuity that a forward-only loop can produce at its splice point. Reversing at each end can make the loop join smoother and reduce an obvious repeating pulse.
fields.practical_application: When editing a sustaining sample, a technician selects ping-pong (bidirectional) loop mode in the sampler and sets loop start and end points at zero crossings so the direction changes are seamless.
common_mistakes: Confusing ping-pong looping with a ping-pong (stereo) delay effect, which is unrelated
Setting loop points off a zero crossing, causing clicks at each direction change
Using it on a sound with strong transients, where the reversed pass sounds unnatural
scenario_contexts: Building a smooth sustaining pad from a short recorded sample
Repairing a looped instrument sample that clicks with a forward-only loop
Creating an evolving texture where the back-and-forth motion is desirable

fields.definition: A sampling technique in which a single recorded sample is played back faster or slower to sound higher or lower in pitch, transposing it across a range of notes rather than recording every note individually.
fields.plain_english: This is a trick where one recorded note is sped up or slowed down to make other notes. Playing it faster makes it higher, and slower makes it lower.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a sampler cover a full keyboard from only a few recordings, saving memory and recording effort. It exists because early samplers had limited memory, and it remains useful for spreading any sample across pitches.
fields.practical_application: A technician assigns a sample to a key zone and lets the sampler transpose it for nearby keys, adding more sample zones when the shifted tone strays too far and starts to sound unnatural.
common_mistakes: Stretching one sample too far, producing the sped-up 'chipmunk' sound because playback speed and pitch change together
Confusing simple pitch-shift sampling with formant-corrected pitch shifting, which preserves timbre
Forgetting to set the correct root key, so notes play at the wrong pitch
scenario_contexts: Mapping a single instrument recording across a keyboard to save memory
Detuning a drum hit up or down for variation
Building a quick playable instrument from one field recording

fields.definition: A recorded sample of a string instrument note produced by plucking the string with a finger (pizzicato articulation) rather than bowing it, giving a short, percussive, quickly decaying tone.
fields.plain_english: A pizzicato sample is a recording of a string being plucked with a finger instead of bowed. It gives a short, punchy note like a plucked guitar string.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the plucked articulation of orchestral strings within a sampled string library so composers can switch between bowed and plucked playing. It exists because pizzicato has a distinct attack and decay that a bowed sample cannot imitate.
fields.practical_application: A technician selects the pizzicato articulation via a keyswitch or separate patch in a string library, then tightens note timing since the short attack exposes any looseness.
common_mistakes: Using bowed (arco) samples where pizzicato is written, losing the plucked attack
Adding long reverb tails that blur the short, defined pizzicato notes
Ignoring round-robin variations, so repeated plucks sound mechanically identical
scenario_contexts: Scoring a light, plucked string passage for film or games
Layering pizzicato strings under a rhythmic pop arrangement
Switching mid-phrase from bowed to plucked strings via a keyswitch

sources: Spitfire Audio / orchestral sample library technical documentation

fields.definition: The maximum number of voices (simultaneous notes or sample playbacks) a sampler or synthesizer can sound at once, set by its hardware or software voice allocation; requests beyond this cap trigger voice stealing.
fields.plain_english: The polyphony limit is the largest number of notes a sampler can play at the same time. Go past it and the oldest notes get cut off to make room.
fields.purpose_function: It bounds the processing and memory the instrument must devote to active voices, keeping playback stable. It exists because every sounding voice consumes CPU and RAM, which are finite.
fields.practical_application: A technician raises or lowers the voice limit to balance rich sustained playing against CPU load, watching for dropped notes and increasing the cap or freezing tracks when voice stealing becomes audible.
common_mistakes: Blaming a bad recording for notes that cut off, when the polyphony limit is causing voice stealing
Forgetting that a held sustain pedal keeps voices alive and quickly exhausts the limit
Setting the limit needlessly high and overloading the CPU
scenario_contexts: Playing dense sustained piano passages with the sustain pedal down
Layering several sampled instruments in one project and running out of voices
Optimizing an older hardware sampler with a low fixed voice count

fields.definition: In a disk-streaming sampler, the initial portion of each sample held in RAM so a note can start instantly while the remainder is streamed from disk; its size trades memory use against reliable streaming under load.
fields.plain_english: A preload buffer is a small first piece of each sound kept ready in memory. It lets a note start right away while the rest is read from the drive.
fields.purpose_function: It hides the delay of reading from storage so notes begin without lag, letting large libraries play from disk instead of loading fully into RAM. It exists because disk access is too slow to fetch a sample's start on demand.
fields.practical_application: A technician tunes the preload buffer size for the drive and project — larger for slow drives or high voice counts to prevent dropouts, smaller to save RAM when memory is tight.
common_mistakes: Setting the preload buffer too small on a slow drive, causing audible dropouts or clicks at note starts
Making it needlessly large and wasting RAM that other instruments need
Confusing the sample preload buffer with the audio interface's I/O buffer, which controls monitoring latency
scenario_contexts: Streaming a large orchestral library from an SSD in a big session
Troubleshooting note-start dropouts on a mechanical hard drive
Balancing RAM between many streamed instruments in one project

fields.definition: Recording audio into a sampler and making it immediately available for triggered playback, so a sound can be captured and performed with little or no processing delay, as opposed to pre-loading edited samples in advance.
fields.plain_english: Real-time sampling means recording a sound and playing it back almost instantly. You can grab a sound and jam with it right away.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a performer capture a source on the spot and play it across the keys during a session or show. It exists to support live remixing, beat-making, and improvisation where waiting to edit a sample is impractical.
fields.practical_application: A technician arms the sampler's input, captures a phrase or hit from a mic or line source, and immediately triggers it from pads or keys, trimming start and end points on the fly.
common_mistakes: Setting record levels too high and clipping the captured sample
Overlooking input latency, so the captured sound sits slightly off the beat
Not trimming the sample start, leaving a gap before the sound triggers
scenario_contexts: A live performer sampling a vocal phrase and replaying it during the set
Beat-making by grabbing a drum hit and mapping it to pads immediately
Capturing a found sound in the field and playing it back on the spot

fields.definition: An oscillator whose waveform phase is reset to a defined start point each time a new note is triggered, so every note begins at the same point in the cycle rather than at a free-running phase.
fields.plain_english: A retriggered oscillator starts its wave over from the beginning each time you press a key. This makes every note begin the same way, so notes sound even.
fields.purpose_function: Resetting phase on each note keeps attacks consistent and predictable, which matters for punchy transients and for keeping layered or stacked oscillators in phase. It exists because a free-running oscillator would start each note at a random phase, varying the attack.
fields.practical_application: A technician enables oscillator retrigger (key sync) when consistent, punchy note starts are needed, and disables it for a looser, more analog-sounding attack that varies note to note.
common_mistakes: Confusing oscillator retrigger with envelope or LFO retrigger, which reset different parts of the voice
Expecting perfectly consistent attacks with retrigger off, when free-running phase varies each note
Leaving retrigger on when a subtly varying, more organic attack is wanted
scenario_contexts: Programming a tight bass patch that needs identical, punchy note attacks
Phase-aligning stacked oscillators so they reinforce rather than cancel
Designing a plucky lead where every note must start the same way

fields.definition: An organized, stored collection of audio samples kept for backup and reuse, typically catalogued with folder structure, naming, and metadata so individual sounds can be located and recalled later.
fields.plain_english: A sample archive is an organized store of your saved sound files. It works like a labeled filing cabinet so you can find and reuse sounds later.
fields.purpose_function: It preserves recorded and collected sounds against loss and makes them easy to search and reload into future projects. It exists because unmanaged sample files quickly become too many to find without a system.
fields.practical_application: A technician maintains an archive on a backed-up drive with consistent naming and tags, so a needed sound can be retrieved and dropped into a sampler without re-recording it.
common_mistakes: Keeping a single unbacked-up copy, risking total loss if the drive fails
Using inconsistent or vague file names, making sounds impossible to find later
Confusing an organized archive with a working library that is actively streamed during playback
scenario_contexts: Backing up a studio's accumulated sound-design recordings
Cataloguing field recordings so they can be searched by tag
Recalling an old project's custom samples for a remix

sources: AES technical documentation on audio file management and metadata
